derivations.claim: By trichotomy, either $y=0$, $y>0$, or $-y>0$. In the first case $y^2=0$. In either positive case, multiplying the positive element by itself gives a positive square; since $(-y)(-y)=y^2$, this proves $y^2\ge0$, with strict inequality when $y\ne0$.
The hypothesis $r^2=x^2+y^2$ and step 1.1 imply $r^2\ge x^2$.
If $x=r$, then $y^2=r^2-x^2=0$. Step 1.1 shows a nonzero $y$ would have $y^2>0$, so $y=0$; and $x=r\ge0$.
If $x\le0$, then $x\le r$ because $r\ge0$. Otherwise $x>0$. If $r<x$, then $x-r>0$ and $x+r>0$, so $x^2-r^2=(x-r)(x+r)>0$, contradicting step 2.1. Hence $x\le r$ in all cases.

Conversely, if $y=0$ and $x\ge0$, the hypotheses give $r^2=x^2$ with $r,x\ge0$. If $r<x$, then $(x-r)(x+r)>0$, contradicting equality of squares; if $x<r$, then $(r-x)(r+x)>0$, the same contradiction. By trichotomy, $r=x$. Equality holds exactly in the stated case.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Use the complex field $\mathbb C$ with conjugation $z\mapsto\overline z$. Fix an integer $N\ge1$. Let $S=\mathbb C^2$ have standard basis $s_1,s_2$. For a complex vector space $W$, its conjugate vector space $\overline W$ consists of symbols $\overline w$ for $w\in W$, with addition $\overline w+\overline v=\overline{w+v}$ and scalar action $\lambda\overline w=\overline{\overline\lambda w}$. Set $\dot S=\overline S$ with dotted basis $\dot s_{\dot1}=\overline{s_1}$ and $\dot s_{\dot2}=\overline{s_2}$. Let $F=\mathbb C^N$ have standard basis $f_1,\ldots,f_N$, and let $F^*$ be its complex-linear dual with dual basis $f^1,\ldots,f^N$ and scalar action $(\lambda\ell)(v)=\lambda\ell(v)$. All tensor products are over $\mathbb C$, with scalar action $\lambda(v\otimes w)=(\lambda v)\otimes w=v\otimes(\lambda w)$ and product bases formed from the displayed bases. Define $\Lambda^2F=(F\otimes_{\mathbb C}F)/\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{v\otimes v:v\in F\}$; its basis is $f_I\wedge f_J$ for $1\le I<J\le N$, with quotient scalar action. Its conjugate $\overline{\Lambda^2F}$ has basis $\overline{f_I\wedge f_J}$ and the conjugate scalar action just defined. For $N=1$ these exterior-square spaces are zero. In the displayed bases, $\mathfrak{sl}(S)=\{A\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(S):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$ and $\mathfrak{sl}(\dot S)=\{B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\dot S):\operatorname{tr}B=0\}$. Put $\epsilon_{12}=\epsilon_{\dot1\dot2}=1$ and $\epsilon_{21}=\epsilon_{\dot2\dot1}=-1$, with zero diagonal. The complex even space is

$$\mathfrak g_{\bar0}=\bigl(\mathfrak{sl}(S)\oplus\mathfrak{sl}(\dot S)\bigr)\oplus V\oplus C_N,\qquad V=S\otimes\dot S,\qquad C_N=\Lambda^2F\oplus\overline{\Lambda^2F}.$$

Write $T_{\alpha\dot\beta}=s_\alpha\otimes\dot s_{\dot\beta}$ for the basis of $V$. The listed central generators form a basis of $C_N$: $Z^{IJ}$ corresponds to $f_I\wedge f_J$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$ to $\overline{f_I\wedge f_J}$ for $1\le I<J\le N$; extend them by antisymmetry in the flavor indices and set their diagonal entries to zero. The complex odd space is

$$\mathfrak g_{\bar1}=(S\otimes F)\oplus(\dot S\otimes F^*),$$

with basis $Q^I_\alpha=s_\alpha\otimes f_I$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}=\dot s_{\dot\alpha}\otimes f^I$. A homogeneous vector has parity $|x|\in\{0,1\}$. The bracket is complex-bilinear, preserves parity, and obeys $[x,y]=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,x]$. Its complete nonzero table, apart from the graded-skew consequences, is

$$[ (A,B),(A',B') ]=([A,A'],[B,B']),\qquad [(A,B),T]= (A\otimes I+I\otimes B)T,$$

$$[(A,B),Q^I_\alpha]=A_\alpha{}^\gamma Q^I_\gamma,\qquad [(A,B),\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}]=B_{\dot\alpha}{}^{\dot\gamma}\bar Q_{\dot\gamma I},$$

$$\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\delta^I{}_J T_{\alpha\dot\beta},\qquad \{Q^I_\alpha,Q^J_\beta\}=2\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ},\qquad \{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=2\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\bar Z_{IJ}.$$

All other brackets vanish: $V$ and $C_N$ are abelian, $C_N$ is central, and $V$ brackets trivially with the odd space. The two antisymmetric factors in each equal-chirality odd bracket make that bracket symmetric in the combined spinor-flavor labels. The Lie-superalgebra and real-form properties are established by the local Jacobi result.

Define a conjugate-linear involution $*$ on the generators by

$$ (A,B)^*=(-\overline B,-\overline A),\quad Q^I_\alpha{}^*=\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\quad \bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}{}^*=Q^I_\alpha,\quad T_{\alpha\dot\beta}^*=T_{\beta\dot\alpha},\quad (Z^{IJ})^*=\bar Z_{IJ},\quad (\bar Z_{IJ})^*=Z^{IJ}.$$

It uses the operator-adjoint convention $[x,y]^*=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[x^*,y^*]$. The associated real Lie superalgebra is the fixed space of the conjugate-linear map $\tau(x)=-x^*$ on even elements and $\tau(x)=i x^*$ on odd elements. Its real Lorentz algebra is the fixed diagonal copy of $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)$; its real translation generators are the $\tau$-fixed skew-Hermitian bispinors. The star-fixed translation coordinates defined below are abstract elements of the complex algebra; their multiples by $i$ form a real basis of the tau-fixed translation space.

For the metric convention $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, put $\sigma^0=I_2$ and

$$\sigma^1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \bar\sigma^0=I_2,\qquad \bar\sigma^j=-\sigma^j.$$

They obey

$$\sigma^\mu\bar\sigma^\nu+\sigma^\nu\bar\sigma^\mu=-2\eta^{\mu\nu}I_2.$$

Define abstract translation coordinates $p_0=(T_{1\dot1}+T_{2\dot2})/2$, $p_1=(T_{1\dot2}+T_{2\dot1})/2$, $p_2=(T_{2\dot1}-T_{1\dot2})/(2i)$, and $p_3=(T_{1\dot1}-T_{2\dot2})/2$. Then $T_{\alpha\dot\beta}=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}p_\mu$, $p_\mu^*=p_\mu$, and $\tau(ip_\mu)=ip_\mu$. A representation of the complex supertranslation algebra $\mathfrak t=V\oplus C_N\oplus\mathfrak g_{\bar1}$ on a graded complex vector space $\mathcal D$ means a parity-preserving complex-linear map $\rho:\mathfrak t\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal D)$ preserving the bracket, where the target bracket is the operator supercommutator. Write $P_\mu=\rho(p_\mu)$ and use the charge symbols for their images. Thus $\rho(T_{\alpha\dot\beta})=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu$ and the represented mixed relation is $\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu\delta^I{}_J$, with $P_\mu=\eta_{\mu\nu}P^\nu$. In a unitary realization the images $P_\mu$ are restrictions of the self-adjoint physical momenta to their common invariant domain; $\rho(ip_\mu)=iP_\mu$, so $-i\rho(ip_\mu)=P_\mu$. In a massive rest fiber $P^\mu=(M,0,0,0)$, so $P_0=-M$ and the mixed anticommutator is $2M\delta_{\alpha\dot\beta}\delta^I{}_J$. Here $N$ counts left Weyl spinors; the scalar central-charge matrix is antisymmetric and therefore vanishes for $N=1$. Tensorial or topological extensions are outside this scalar-central-charge algebra. The convention uses natural units $\hbar=c=1$; translation and central-charge generators have mass dimension one and supercharges have mass dimension one-half.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the complex Hilbert-space convention that the inner product is linear in its first variable and conjugate-linear in its second. Let $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\sigma^0=I_2$, $\sigma^1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Define $\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)=\{H\in M_2(\mathbb C):H^\dagger=H\}$ and $\Phi:\mathbb R^{1,3}\to\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)$ by $\Phi(x)=-\sigma^\mu x_\mu$. For $g\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)=\{g\in M_2(\mathbb C):\det g=1\}$, define $\Lambda_g$ by $\Phi(\Lambda_gx)=g\Phi(x)g^\dagger$; the real-linear map $\Phi$ is an isomorphism because $I_2,\sigma^1,\sigma^2,\sigma^3$ form a basis of $\operatorname{Herm}_2(\mathbb C)$. Since $\det g=1$, $\det(g\Phi(x)g^\dagger)=\det g\,\det\Phi(x)\,\overline{\det g}=\det\Phi(x)$; with $\det\Phi(x)=-\eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu$, this proves determinant and Lorentz-form preservation. These maps satisfy $\Lambda_{I_2}=I$ and $\Lambda_g\Lambda_h=\Lambda_{gh}$: applying $\Phi$ to the left side gives $gh\Phi(x)h^\dagger g^\dagger=(gh)\Phi(x)(gh)^\dagger$, and injectivity of $\Phi$ gives the equality; in particular $\Lambda_{g^{-1}}=\Lambda_g^{-1}$. Thus $g\mapsto\Lambda_g$ is a group action, so it defines the semidirect-product structure below. Congruence by $g$ preserves positive-semidefinite Hermitian matrices, so $\Lambda_g$ preserves the chosen future cone. Let $\Lambda_g^\vee$ be the dual action on covectors, $(\Lambda_g^\vee p)(x)=p(\Lambda_g^{-1}x)$. The spin-cover Poincare group is $\mathcal P=\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)\ltimes_\Lambda\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with product $(g,a)(h,b)=(gh,a+\Lambda_gb)$.

A **positive unitary super-Poincare representation** in this item is the following data. It includes a nonzero complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ and a bounded self-adjoint grading operator $\Gamma$ with $\Gamma^2=I$; write $\mathcal H^\pm=\ker(\Gamma\mp I)$. Give $\mathcal P=\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)\ltimes_\Lambda\mathbb R^{1,3}$ the product topology from the usual matrix topology and Euclidean topology. Let $\mathcal U(\mathcal H)=\{V\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H):V^*V=VV^*=I\}$. The data include a map $U:\mathcal P\to\mathcal U(\mathcal H)$ satisfying $U(1,0)=I$ and $U((g,a)(h,b))=U(g,a)U(h,b)$ for all $(g,a),(h,b)\in\mathcal P$, with $U(g,a)\Gamma=\Gamma U(g,a)$. Require the orbit map $(g,a)\mapsto U(g,a)\psi$ to be norm-continuous for every $\psi\in\mathcal H$; this is strong continuity. The data also include a regular projection-valued measure $E$ on the Borel subsets of the covector space $(\mathbb R^{1,3})^*$ such that

$$U(1,a)=\Phi_E(p\mapsto e^{i p(a)}),\qquad U(g,0)E(B)U(g,0)^*=E(\Lambda_g^\vee B),\qquad E(\mathcal C_+^*)=I,$$

where $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel PVM integral, $\mathcal C_+^*=\{p:p^0=-p_0\ge |\vec p|\}$ is the closed future cone in covector coordinates, and $p(a)=p_\mu a^\mu$. The PVM functional calculus makes every translation unitary commute with every $E(B)$. For each coordinate define the self-adjoint translation generator

$$P_\mu=p_\mu(E),\qquad D(P_\mu)=\left\{\psi\in\mathcal H:\int |p_\mu|^2\,dE_\psi(p)<\infty\right\},\qquad E_\psi(B)=\langle E(B)\psi,\psi\rangle.$$

Here $p_\mu(E)$ is the unbounded PVM integral with its truncation domain; the real-valued integral is self-adjoint under Countable Choice. Thus $P^0=\eta^{0\nu}P_\nu$ is nonnegative. The joint PVM is part of the representation data; no joint spectral measure is inferred from formal commutators on a dense domain.

For each $I,\alpha$, the supercharge $Q^I_\alpha$ is a closed densely defined operator on $\mathcal H$ and $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I}=(Q^I_\alpha)^*$ is its actual Hilbert adjoint, with exactly the adjoint domain. Require the grading to preserve each actual charge domain and each closed charge to be odd there: $\Gamma D(Q^I_\alpha)=D(Q^I_\alpha)$ and $Q^I_\alpha\Gamma\psi=-\Gamma Q^I_\alpha\psi$ for every $\psi\in D(Q^I_\alpha)$, with the same two conditions for $(Q^I_\alpha)^*$ on $D((Q^I_\alpha)^*)$. The central generators $Z^{IJ}$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}$, which belong to the even part of the algebra, are represented by closed densely defined operators with $\bar Z_{IJ}=(Z^{IJ})^*$ as an actual Hilbert adjoint; require $\Gamma D(Z^{IJ})=D(Z^{IJ})$ and $Z^{IJ}\Gamma\psi=\Gamma Z^{IJ}\psi$ on $D(Z^{IJ})$, with the corresponding conditions for $\bar Z_{IJ}$ on its actual domain. On a common dense graded linear domain $\mathcal D$, contained in the domains of every generator product in the bracket table, the operator supercommutator is the displayed algebra bracket. In particular,

$$\{Q^I_\alpha,\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=-2\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu\delta^I{}_J,\qquad \{Q^I_\alpha,Q^J_\beta\}=2\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}Z^{IJ},\qquad \{\bar Q_{\dot\alpha I},\bar Q_{\dot\beta J}\}=2\epsilon_{\dot\alpha\dot\beta}\bar Z_{IJ}.$$

The domain $\mathcal D$ is invariant under those generators and under $U(\mathcal P)$. Explicitly, these restrictions define the complex-linear supertranslation representation $\rho_{\mathcal D}:\mathfrak t\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal D)$: it sends the abstract $p_\mu$ to $P_\mu|_{\mathcal D}$ and each abstract supercharge or central generator to its named operator restricted to $\mathcal D$. Invariance of $\mathcal D$ makes these endomorphisms, and the assumed bracket identities make $\rho_{\mathcal D}$ bracket-preserving. In particular, $\rho_{\mathcal D}(T_{\alpha\dot\beta})=\sigma^\mu_{\alpha\dot\beta}P_\mu|_{\mathcal D}$ and $-i\rho_{\mathcal D}(ip_\mu)=P_\mu|_{\mathcal D}$. The even group acts on the charge domains exactly: for every $g\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C)$, conjugation by $U(g,0)$ sends each closed charge to the corresponding fundamental or dotted spinor transform as an equality of operators, including equality of domains. The central generators transform as Lorentz scalars, commute with translations, and commute on $\mathcal D$ with all supercharges; these relations also include their domain invariance.

For every Borel set $B\subseteq(\mathbb R^{1,3})^*$ and every charge $Q$ or $Q^*$, require the reducing-projection/domain conditions

$$E(B)D(Q)\subseteq D(Q),\qquad Q E(B)\psi=E(B)Q\psi\quad(\psi\in D(Q)),$$

and the same conditions with $Q^*$ in place of $Q$. Require also $\Gamma E(B)=E(B)\Gamma$ for every Borel $B$. In particular this supplies integrated translation covariance with domain invariance; a relation $[P_\mu,Q]=0$ on a common core alone is not substituted for it. A closed complex-linear subspace $K$ is graded when $\Gamma K=K$, equivalently $K=(K\cap\mathcal H^+)\oplus(K\cap\mathcal H^-)$. Such a subspace is invariant when $U(g,a)K=K$ for all $(g,a)\in\mathcal P$ and each charge and adjoint maps $D(Q)\cap K$ into $K$, with those intersections dense in $K$. The representation is irreducible when its only such invariant subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$.

Let a positive unitary representation of the four-dimensional extended super-Poincare algebra act on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, with common invariant product domain $\mathcal D$, translation generators $P^\mu$, supercharges $Q^I_\alpha$, and actual Hilbert adjoints $(Q^I_\alpha)^*$, using metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\sigma^0=I_2$, and natural units $\hbar=c=1$. A **rest-frame ground-state vector** is a vector $\Omega\in\mathcal D$ such that $\|\Omega\|=1$, there is a real number $E_\Omega$ with $P^0\Omega=E_\Omega\Omega$ and $P^j\Omega=0$ for $j=1,2,3$, and

$$\langle P^0\psi,\psi\rangle\ge E_\Omega\|\psi\|^2\qquad(\psi\in D(P^0)).$$

Such a vector is called a **global supersymmetry vacuum state** in the representation. Its vacuum energy is the eigenvalue $E_\Omega$, with units of mass in natural units; it is not an energy density. The vector is **boundary-neutral** when $Z^{IJ}\Omega=0$ and $\bar Z_{IJ}\Omega=0$ for every central generator, **supersymmetry-invariant** when $Q^I_\alpha\Omega=(Q^I_\alpha)^*\Omega=0$ for every $I,\alpha$, and **supersymmetry-noninvariant** when at least one of these vectors is nonzero. These are separate predicates: boundary neutrality does not define supersymmetry invariance. The definition does not assert that any such vector exists or that a constant field configuration is allowed by a separate field-model boundary condition.

derivations.claim: In the Countable-Choice representation setup [A1, F2], sum the mixed anticommutator in [F1] over the equal spinor labels $\alpha=\dot\beta$ and over $I=1,\ldots,N$. The Kronecker delta leaves one copy for each flavor, and the Pauli-matrix traces give $\sum_{I=1}^{N}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{2}\{Q^I_\alpha,(Q^I_\alpha)^*\}=-2N\sum_{\mu=0}^{3}\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^\mu)P_\mu=-4N P_0=4N P^0$. The last equality uses $P_0=-P^0$ for the stated metric.

Apply the operator identity from step 1.1 to $\Omega$ and take its inner product with $\Omega$. The common product domain in [F2] makes both products defined. Since the inner product is linear in its first variable and $(Q^I_\alpha)^*$ is the actual adjoint, $\langle Q^I_\alpha(Q^I_\alpha)^*\Omega,\Omega\rangle=\|(Q^I_\alpha)^*\Omega\|^2$ and $\langle (Q^I_\alpha)^*Q^I_\alpha\Omega,\Omega\rangle=\|Q^I_\alpha\Omega\|^2$. The right side is $4N\langle P^0\Omega,\Omega\rangle=4NE_\Omega$ by [F3] and normalization. This proves the asserted sum-of-norms identity.

Every summand in step 2.1 is nonnegative, so $E_\Omega\ge0$. A finite sum of nonnegative real numbers is zero exactly when every summand is zero; hence $E_\Omega=0$ exactly when all $Q^I_\alpha\Omega$ and $(Q^I_\alpha)^*\Omega$ vanish, which is precisely supersymmetry invariance by [F3]. If the state is noninvariant, at least one squared norm is strictly positive, so the identity and $4N>0$ imply $E_\Omega>0$. The argument contains no boundary-neutrality assumption.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 1.1: N>=1 makes the supercharge sum have exactly 2N index pairs, so an empty flavor sum is excluded before division by 4N. Normalization ||Omega||=1 also excludes the zero state and an empty Hilbert-state sector; the theorem remains conditional on their existence.
Step 3.1 proves the zero-energy iff condition.
N=1 is included because step 3.1 uses only 4N>0.
When every charge and adjoint annihilates Ω, the identity in step 2.1 gives EΩ=0.

citations.quote:
Use the physical action brackets $[U]_D=-I_D(U)/4$ and $[Y]_F=I_F(Y)/2$ from Physical superspace action brackets and canonical chiral components, with raw mathematical coefficient integrals $I_D,I_F$ unchanged. Physical chiral components obey $\psi_{\mathrm{raw}}=\sqrt2\psi$ and $F_{\mathrm{raw}}=2F$. All physical action and coupling formulas below use these brackets and physical component names; adding Hermitian conjugation applies only to the F action and occurs once.

Use oriented and time-oriented Minkowski spacetime $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with coordinates $x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and natural units $\hbar=c=1$. Let $n\geq1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be an open set containing $0$, let $K:U\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, and require the Hermitian matrix $g_{i\bar j}(z,\bar z)=\partial_i\partial_{\bar j}K(z,\bar z)$ to be positive definite at every point of $U$. Let $W:U\to\mathbb C$ be smooth and holomorphic, where holomorphic means $\partial_{\bar i}W=0$ for every $i$, using the Wirtinger derivatives of the Kähler coordinate-patch definition; write $W_i=\partial_iW$. These data specify the Kähler coordinate patch and holomorphic superpotential of the model.

For these classical fields, take a finite-dimensional exterior algebra $\mathcal G$ over $\mathbb C$ on ordered odd generators $\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_m$ for $m\geq0$, with componentwise complex addition and multiplication modulo $\zeta_a^2=0$ and $\zeta_a\zeta_b=-\zeta_b\zeta_a$. Give it the conjugate-linear operation $(c\zeta_{i_1}\cdots\zeta_{i_r})^*=\bar c\zeta_{i_r}\cdots\zeta_{i_1}$, so $\zeta_a^*=\zeta_a$, $(uv)^*=v^*u^*$ and $(u^*)^*=u$. Reversing twice proves involutivity, and reversing the defining relations preserves them; thus this is a well-defined parity-preserving anti-automorphism. Write $\mathcal G_{\bar0},\mathcal G_{\bar1}$ for its even and odd subspaces, and use its degree-zero projection $b:\mathcal G\to\mathbb C$. Form the graded tensor product $\mathcal B=\mathcal G\otimes_{\mathbb C}\Lambda_4$ with the superspace Grassmann algebra, and let $\mathfrak J$ be the ideal of elements with zero total degree-zero part. Then $\mathfrak J^{m+5}=0$. For an even superfield $\Phi^i$, its body is its image under the augmentation $\mathcal B\to\mathbb C$ that applies $b$ and sends all superspace generators to zero; denote that ordinary scalar component by $\phi^i(x)$. Write $\bar\Phi^{\bar i}=(\Phi^i)^*$, $\nu^i=\Phi^i-\phi^i$, and $\bar\nu^{\bar i}=\bar\Phi^{\bar i}-\bar\phi^{\bar i}$; these differences lie in $\mathfrak J$. Define the smooth function's value on the full superfields by the finite nilpotent Taylor convention

$$K(\bar\Phi,\Phi):=\sum_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N^n\\|\alpha|+|\beta|\leq m+4}}\frac{(\partial_z^\alpha\partial_{\bar z}^\beta K)(\phi,\bar\phi)}{\alpha!\,\beta!}(\nu)^\alpha(\bar\nu)^\beta,$$

where $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$, $\beta!=\prod_i\beta_i!$, $\nu^\alpha=\prod_i(\nu^i)^{\alpha_i}$, $(\bar\nu)^\beta=\prod_i(\bar\nu^{\bar i})^{\beta_i}$, $\partial_z^\alpha=\prod_i\partial_i^{\alpha_i}$, $\partial_{\bar z}^\beta=\prod_i\partial_{\bar i}^{\beta_i}$, and the coefficient derivatives are evaluated at $(\phi(x),\bar\phi(x))$. Define the holomorphic superfield evaluation and its derivatives by the finite Taylor rule at the scalar body,

$$W(\Phi)(x,\theta,\bar\theta):=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq m+4}\frac{(\partial_z^\alpha W)(\phi(x))}{\alpha!}(\nu)^\alpha,\qquad W_i(\Phi):=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq m+4}\frac{(\partial_z^\alpha\partial_iW)(\phi(x))}{\alpha!}(\nu)^\alpha.$$

All terms beyond these finite sums vanish because $\mathfrak J^{m+5}=0$; the rule for $K$ is the Taylor extension of a smooth real function in its $z,\bar z$ variables, and the rule for $W$ uses only its holomorphic Wirtinger derivatives.

For each $i=1,\ldots,n$, the full formal physical components are smooth maps $a^i,\mathcal F^i:M\to\mathcal G_{\bar0}$ and $\psi^i_\alpha:M\to\mathcal G_{\bar1}$, with compact support in spacetime $M$: equivalently each coefficient of each exterior-basis monomial is a compactly supported smooth complex function of $x$. Require the scalar body $\phi^i=b(a^i)$ to lie in $U$ jointly. The lowest chiral coefficient is $a^i$, not merely its body $\phi^i$; it may have even nilpotent terms. In the physical normalization definition instantiate its scalar and auxiliary component symbols by $a^i$ and $\mathcal F^i$, respectively:

$$\Phi^i(y,\theta)=a^i(y)+\sqrt2\theta^\alpha\psi^i_\alpha(y)+2\theta^1\theta^2\mathcal F^i(y),\qquad y=x+i\theta\sigma\bar\theta.$$

Barred component fields mean the specified coefficient involution, so $\bar a^{\bar i}=(a^i)^*$ and $\overline{\mathcal F}^{\bar i}=(\mathcal F^i)^*$; barred fermions are likewise the conjugates of the coefficient maps. On $\mathcal B$ use the supplier's graded-tensor involution, including $\theta^*=\bar\theta$ and reversal of all factors. The formal action has values in the even fixed real subspace of $\mathcal G$; no order or nonnegativity is assigned to nilpotent elements.

The supersymmetry parameters $\epsilon^\alpha,\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}$ are constant odd coefficients, in $\mathcal G$ or a finite exterior extension equipped with the same involution. The adopted variation is $\delta\Phi^i=(\epsilon^\alpha Q_\alpha+\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}\bar Q_{\dot\alpha})\Phi^i$ with the chiral-superfield supercharges. Formal parameter components may be treated independently for the algebraic identities; a conjugation-preserving variation in this left-parameter convention has $\bar\epsilon^{\dot\alpha}=-(\epsilon^\alpha)^*$ and $\delta\bar\Phi=(\delta\Phi)^*$. Indeed $\delta\theta=\epsilon$ and $\delta\bar\theta=-\bar\epsilon$ then commute with the chosen involution. The full even coefficient spaces for $a$ and $\mathcal F$ are retained under these transformations; the ordinary bosonic slice below need not be invariant. The engineering dimensions are $[x^\mu]=-1$, $[\theta]=[\bar\theta]=-1/2$, $[a^i]=1$, $[\psi^i]=3/2$, $[\mathcal F^i]=2$, $[K]=2$, and $[W]=3$ in mass units.

Adopt the classical action

$$S_{\mathrm{WZ}}=\int_M d^4x\left([K(\bar\Phi,\Phi)]_D+[W(\Phi)]_F+\mathrm{h.c.}\right),$$

where only the chiral F action has a Hermitian-conjugate partner and the D bracket is real; both physical brackets are the fixed multiples of the earlier raw ordered measures. The **ordinary bosonic sector** is the restriction $\psi=0$, $a=\phi\in\mathbb C^n$ and $\mathcal F=F\in\mathbb C^n$ with all positive-degree coefficient-algebra components set to zero; $\phi:M\to U$ and $F:M\to\mathbb C^n$ remain smooth and compactly supported in $M$. Thus taking this sector commutes with the degree-zero augmentation, but it is a restriction for evaluating a bosonic action, not an assertion of off-shell supersymmetry closure on a purely complex field space. The component conversion below gives its complete bosonic Lagrangian, up to the displayed spacetime divergence,

$$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{bos}}=-g_{i\bar j}(\phi,\bar\phi)\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi^i\partial_\nu\bar\phi^{\bar j}+g_{i\bar j}(\phi,\bar\phi)F^i\bar F^{\bar j}+F^iW_i(\phi)+\bar F^{\bar j}\overline{W_j(\phi)}+\tfrac14\Box K(\phi,\bar\phi),\qquad\Box=\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu.$$

Its bosonic zero-derivative auxiliary terms are therefore precisely

$$\mathcal L_F=g_{i\bar j}(\phi,\bar\phi)F^i\bar F^{\bar j}+F^iW_i(\phi)+\bar F^{\bar j}\overline{W_j(\phi)}.$$

Only this ordinary complex sector is used for the ordered real scalar-potential and minimization conclusions. An arbitrary even $\mathcal G$-valued auxiliary field remains valid in the full formal model, but is not a vector in an ordered positive-definite complex metric space.

The canonical Wess–Zumino model is the special case $U=\mathbb C^n$, $K(z,\bar z)=\sum_i\bar z^{\bar i}z^i$, and hence $g_{i\bar j}=\delta_{i\bar j}$. This is an adopted classical formulation and normalization, not a deduction that nature realizes the model.

Use the rigid N=1 Kähler sigma-model action with scalar coordinates $z=(z^1,\ldots,z^n)\in U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, smooth real Kähler potential $K$, positive-definite Hermitian metric $g_{i\bar j}=\partial_i\partial_{\bar j}K$, holomorphic superpotential $W$, and complex algebraic auxiliary fields $F^i$. Use the ordinary complex bosonic sector of that postulate: all positive-degree coefficient-algebra components and fermions are set to zero, and the full formal even auxiliary coefficient is restricted to the complex field $F^i$. This restriction is for the potential calculation and does not assert supersymmetry closure on the restricted slice. With spacetime derivatives set to zero, write $W_i=\partial_iW(z)$ and $\bar W_{\bar j}=\partial_{\bar j}\overline{W(z)}$. The auxiliary Lagrangian is

$$\mathcal L_F=g_{i\bar j}F^i\bar F^{\bar j}+F^iW_i+\bar F^{\bar j}\bar W_{\bar j}.$$

Let $g^{i\bar j}$ be the inverse Hermitian matrix. The algebraic field equation is $F^i=-g^{i\bar j}\bar W_{\bar j}$, and eliminating $F$ gives the nonnegative scalar-potential contribution

$$V_F=g^{i\bar j}W_i\bar W_{\bar j}\geq0.$$

For the canonical Kähler potential $K=\sum_i\bar z^{\bar i}z^i$, this becomes $V_F=\sum_i|W_i|^2$. The simple sum is specific to that metric; for a noncanonical Kähler metric the inverse matrix in the displayed formula is required. This statement concerns the classical F-term sector only and does not include gauge D-terms or quantum corrections.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Every $z=a+bi\in\mathbb C$ has a square root. If $b\ne0$, one square root is
$$u+vi,\qquad u=\sqrt{\frac{|z|+a}{2}},\qquad v=\frac{b}{2u}.$$
If $b=0$, one may take $\sqrt a$ when $a\ge0$, and
$i\sqrt{-a}$ when $a<0$.
For $x,y,r\in\mathbb R$ with $r\ge0$ and $r^2=x^2+y^2$, one has $x\le r$. Equality holds exactly when $y=0$ and $x\ge0$.

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.
